citation.title: Beyond LATE: Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect with an Instrumental Variable

standing_assumptions:
The article is P. M. Aronow and A. Carnegie, ‘Beyond LATE: Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect with an Instrumental Variable’, Political Analysis 21 (2013), pp. 492–506. Printed page = PDF page + 491 (printed p. 492 is PDF p. 1). The official supplement (‘Supporting Information Online Appendix A: Simulation Studies’) is paginated A1–A12 and supplement PDF page k is page Ak. The article states no numbered theorem, proposition or lemma; its formal content is the displayed equations (1)–(14), Assumptions 1–3 and the statements in running text and footnotes quoted below. Everything quoted from the article and the supplement was read from the page images (the staged 110 dpi images and 250 dpi renderings of the same PDF pages). Code and package text have no page image and are transcribed from the staged source files; each such passage is marked.
(S1) Setting and potential outcomes. p. 494 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.2: “We now move to the Neyman-Rubin potential outcomes framework, focusing on the case of a binary IV (or treatment assignment) $Z$ and a binary endogenous treatment variable (or treatment received) $D$. Suppose that we have a sample consisting of $n$ units (indexed $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$) independently drawn with equal probability from some large population of interest. For unit $i$, let $Y_{0i}$ be the outcome if untreated, $D_i = 0$, and let $Y_{1i}$ be the outcome if treated, $D_i = 1$. The treatment effect for a given unit $i$ is the difference between unit $i$’s outcomes in both possible states of the world, $Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$. Similarly, we may define $D_{0i}$ as the treatment condition of unit $i$ when assigned to control, $Z_i = 0$, and $D_{1i}$ as the treatment condition of unit $i$ when assigned to treatment, $Z_i = 1$. We will show that the causal estimand recovered by IV estimation will not generally be the ATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$, but will instead be the LATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0)$.”
(S2) Types. pp. 494–495 (PDF pp. 3–4): “Following Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996), the population may be divided into four groups: always-takers, never-takers, compliers, and defiers. Always-takers are units that receive treatment regardless of whether they are assigned to treatment or control, so that $D_{0i} = 1$ and $D_{1i} = 1$. Conversely, never-takers do not receive treatment regardless of their treatment assignment, so that $D_{0i} = 0$ and $D_{1i} = 0$. Compliers receive treatment if assigned to treatment and do not receive treatment if assigned to control, so that $D_{0i} = 0$ and $D_{1i} = 1$ (or $D_{1i} > D_{0i}$). Defiers receive treatment if assigned to control and do not receive treatment if assigned to treatment, so that $D_{0i} = 1$ and $D_{1i} = 0$ (or $D_{0i} > D_{1i}$).”
(S3) The five IV assumptions. p. 495 (PDF p. 4): “Using an IV estimator, we may estimate the LATE using five assumptions, as explicated by Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996). First, we assume that the exclusion restriction is valid, or that $Z_i$ only affects $Y_i$ through $D_i$. Second, we assume that $Z_i$ to some degree predicts $D_i$. Third, we invoke the stable unit treatment value assumption, which states that the potential outcomes $D_{0i}$, $D_{1i}$, $Y_{0i}$, and $Y_{1i}$ are fixed and unrelated to the particular arrangement of assignment and treatment statuses. Fourth, we assume that the population contains no defiers, i.e., $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$. Fifth, we assume that $Z_i$ is randomly assigned and thus independent of all potential outcomes.”
(S4) Rendering of (S1)–(S3) used in every target (the article prints no display for it; all validators use it). The observed variables are $D = D_0 + Z(D_1 - D_0)$ and $Y = Y_0 + D(Y_1 - Y_0)$ (exclusion and SUTVA); relevance is $\mathrm{E}(D|Z=1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z=0) \neq 0$; no defiers is $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$; random assignment is: $Z$ is independent of $(D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$, and of $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$ where covariates appear (p. 496: “so that $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$”), with $0 < \Pr(Z = 1) < 1$. Abbreviations used in the targets and not in the article: $\tau = Y_1 - Y_0$ and $C = \mathbf{1}\{D_1 > D_0\}$.
(S5) SEM framework. p. 493 (PDF p. 2), Section 2.1: “The SEM interpretation of IV estimation posits a linear, additive relationship between an outcome variable ($Y_i$), an endogenous treatment variable ($D_i$), covariates ($Q_{1i}, Q_{2i}....Q_{Ki}$), and an unobserved error term ($u_i$) for each unit $i$, such that $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \lambda_1 Q_{1i} + \lambda_2 Q_{2i} + .... + \lambda_K Q_{Ki} + u_i. \qquad (1)$$” p. 494 (PDF p. 3): “The first equation, or the “first stage,” is a regression of the endogenous variable on the instrument and covariates: $$D_i = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 Z_i + \delta_1 Q_{1i} + \delta_2 Q_{2i} + .... + \delta_K Q_{Ki} + e_i, \qquad (2)$$ where $e_i$ is a second unobserved error term. [...] Given the model in equations (1) and (2), the SEM IV framework relies on two main assumptions for consistency. First, the correlation between $Z_i$ and $u_i$ must approach zero as $n$ grows. Second, the covariance between $Z_i$ and $D_i$ must converge to a nonzero quantity as $n$ grows. Note, however, that whereas the endogenous variable and covariates in equation (1) are indexed by the subscript $i$, their coefficients (the βs and λs) are not. In other words, the SEM framework assumes constant treatment effects, so that the effect of the treatment is identical for each unit $i$.”
(S6) Compliance score and nested model. p. 496 (PDF p. 5), Section 3.1: “The compliance score is a latent pretreatment covariate that represents the probability of being a complier, conditional on a unit’s pretreatment covariate profile $\mathbf{X}$ (so that $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$). The compliance score for unit $i$, $P_{Ci} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i)$, where $\mathbf{x}_i$ is the covariate vector for unit $i$.” Equations (5) and (6), p. 496: $$P_{A,C,i} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0 \cup D_0 = 1|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}), \qquad (5)$$ “where $P_{A,C,i}$ is the conditional probability that unit $i$ is either a complier or an always-taker, $\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}$ is a vector of coefficients to be estimated, and $F(\cdot)$ is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for an arbitrary distribution. For the purposes of this article, we use a probit model, so $F(\cdot) = \Phi(\cdot)$, where $\Phi$ is the Normal CDF. Second, we similarly specify $$P_{A|A,C,i} = \Pr(D_0 = 1|D_1 > D_0 \cup D_0 = 1, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}), \qquad (6)$$ where $P_{A|A,C,i}$ is the conditional probability that unit $i$ is an always-taker conditional on it being either an always-taker or a complier, and $\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}$ are coefficients to be estimated.” Equation (7), p. 497 (PDF p. 6): “[...] our third assumption: $D_i$ is Bernoulli distributed. Then the likelihood for any unit $i$, $$L(P_{A|A,C,i}, P_{A,C,i}|D, Z) = (P_{A,C,i}(1 - P_{A|A,C,i})Z_i + P_{A,C,i}P_{A|A,C,i})^{D_i}(1 - P_{A,C,i}(1 - P_{A|A,C,i})Z_i - P_{A,C,i}P_{A|A,C,i})^{1-D_i}. \qquad (7)$$ Combining equations (5), (6), and (7), $L(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}|D, Z) = \Pi_{i=1}^{n}((F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))Z_i + F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))^{D_i}(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))Z_i - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))^{1-D_i})$. Thus the ML estimate of $\{\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\}$, $$\{\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \hat\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\} = \underset{\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}},\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}}{\mathrm{argmax}}\left[L(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}|D, Z)\right].$$ After estimating $\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}$ and $\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}$, we may estimate the compliance score for unit $i$, $$\hat{P}_{Ci} = \widehat{\Pr}(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})).$$” (On the page this display is followed by a superscript 3, which is the marker of footnote 3 and not an exponent.) The displays between (6) and (7) that carry the misprints of finding P029-E009 are transcribed in P029-T18.
(S7) ICSW estimator. p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.3: “In the bivariate case (when there are no covariates), the estimator is simple. Define $\hat{w}_{Ci} = 1/\hat{P}_{Ci}$. The ICSW estimator $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} =$ $$\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iY_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i) - (\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)Y_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i))}{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iD_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i) - (\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)D_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i))}.$$ An equivalent estimator may be derived using weighted 2SLS (with weights $\hat{w}_{Ci}$). As with the simple 2SLS case, covariates may also be included to reduce sampling variability without any consequence for the asymptotic bias of the estimator.”
(S8) Assumptions 1–3. p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.4: “In order to consistently estimate the ATE using ICSW, three additional assumptions are required. In the appendix, we demonstrate that ICSW is consistent under Assumptions 1–3, along with the IV assumptions and suitable regularity conditions.” p. 499 (PDF p. 8): “Assumption 1. Latent ignorability of compliance with respect to treatment effect heterogeneity (Frangakis and Rubin 1999; Esterling, Neblo, and Lazer 2011) holds. Assumption 1 entails that, for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$: the expected value of the treatment effect conditional on a covariate profile is equal to the expected value of the treatment effect conditional on a covariate profile and compliance. Put simply, the ATE for all units with a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$ is equal to the ATE for compliers with a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$.” p. 500 (PDF p. 9): “Assumption 2. Consistency of $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ for $P_{Ci}$. Assumption 2 amounts to requiring proper specification of the ML estimator. Application of a flexible parametrization of the covariates in $\mathbf{X}$, as is possible with large samples, will necessarily yield consistency, so long as the rate of growth in the number of estimated parameters is sufficiently slow in $n$. In the case of a saturated model and $F(.)$ as the normal CDF, $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ will be unbiased for the conditional probability of compliance.” p. 500: “Assumption 3. For all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$, $\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) \in (\epsilon, 1]$, where $\epsilon > 0$. Note that IV estimation already requires the assumption of nonzero compliance in the full population, and we generalize this assumption to every covariate profile.”
(S9) Appendix notation. p. 504 (PDF p. 13): “For clarity, we remove $i$ subscripts to denote all units subject to any conditional probabilities articulated.” p. 499 (PDF p. 8): “where $f(.)$ is the population pdf of $\mathbf{X}$, $g(.)$ is the subpopulation pdf of $\mathbf{X}$ among compliers, and $\Omega = \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$.” The article writes integrals against the density $f$; the validators’ witnesses use covariates with finitely many values, for which $f(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ and the integrals are sums.
(S10) Simulation designs (supplement). Supplement p. A1, ‘Baseline Data Generating Process’ (as printed; the misprints are the subject of P029-T19): $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i \sim \mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$; $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \sim \mathrm{U}(-2, 2)$; $AC_i = \mathbf{I}[2 + a + bX1_i + cX2_i + dX3_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 3)]$; $A_i = \mathbf{I}[-2 + e + fX1_i + gX2_i + hX3_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 3)]AC_i$; $C_i = AC_i - A_i$; $D_i = D_iZ_i + A_i$; $Y_{0i} = 5AC_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$; $\tau_i = 5 \times (1 + X1_i + X2_i + X3_i)$; $Y_i = Y_{0i} + \tau_iD_i$. “We observe and use $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$ both as covariates in 2SLS, and for the compliance score model.” Supplement p. A2, under the heading ‘Heterogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’: “Same as baseline, except: $X1'_i, X2'_i, X3'_i \sim U(-1, 1)$ are the observed covariates, which are entirely independent from $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$.” Under the heading ‘Homogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’: “Same as the previous DGP, except: $\tau_i = 5, \forall i$.”

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Table A3 and the ‘Noise (Homogeneous)’ panel of Figure A3, corrected scoring rule: RMSE about the constant effect 5, with the exact relation to the coded statistic
canonical_claim.location: Supplement pp. A2, A5–A7; deposited code ‘Simulations Misspecification Noise 6-20.R’, lines 124–135, and ‘Sim-Display Misspec.R’, lines 59–70
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text (validated.json, P029-E011, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Score homogeneous-noise estimates in rows 9-12 against 5 in both reporting scripts, then regenerate the corresponding table and figure. Retain heterogeneous scoring against row 1. Exact historical numerical corrections require the simulation arrays or a rerun.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
(a) [The target] In the design ‘Homogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’ the potential outcomes of unit $i$ are $Y_{0i}$ and $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i} + 5$, so $Y_{1i} - Y_{0i} = 5$ for every unit; hence for every sample of size $n \ge 1$ the sample average effect $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (Y_{1i} - Y_{0i})$ equals $5$, the population ATE $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$ equals $5$, and $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0) = 5$ whenever $\Pr(D_1 > D_0) > 0$.
(b) [The corrected statistic] For estimator $j$ and replicates $r = 1, \ldots, R$: $\mathrm{RMSE}_j = \sqrt{\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(t_{jr} - 5)^2}$.
(c) [The coded benchmark] Let $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, be $3n$ independent $\mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$ variables and $B = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}5(1 + X1_i + X2_i + X3_i)$. Then $\mathrm{E}(U) = 0$ and $\mathrm{E}(U^2) = 1/3$ for $U \sim \mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$, $\mathrm{E}(B) = 5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 25/n$.
(d) [Exact relation between the two squared errors] For all real $t$ and $B$: $(t - B)^2 - (t - 5)^2 = (B - 5)^2 - 2(t - 5)(B - 5)$. Hence for any finite run $\frac{1}{R}\sum_r (t_{jr} - B_r)^2 - \frac{1}{R}\sum_r (t_{jr} - 5)^2 = \frac{1}{R}\sum_r (B_r - 5)^2 - \frac{2}{R}\sum_r (t_{jr} - 5)(B_r - 5)$, and if $t$ and $B$ have finite second moments with $\mathrm{E}(B) = 5$, $\mathrm{E}(t - B)^2 - \mathrm{E}(t - 5)^2 = \mathrm{Var}(B) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(t, B)$.
(e) [The sign of the discrepancy is not determined by $\mathrm{Var}(B)$] There are admissible inputs with $(t - B)^2 - (t - 5)^2 = 1$ and admissible inputs with $(t - B)^2 - (t - 5)^2 = -1$: P029-T5(b) and (c).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The designs and the uniform covariates: (S10). The coded statistic, the meaning of rows 1 and 9–12 and of $B_r$: P029-T5. Not in the supplement: the RMSE formula (none is printed), and (c)–(e), which are the adjudicating validator's (derivation.md, sections 1, 2 and 6).
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: replace `simoutput[1,isN]` by 5 in the six rows-9:12 formulas of each of the two scripts and regenerate Table A3 and the panel; repair cost none (no assumption, estimand or fit changes; summaries must be recomputed). The corrected numbers themselves are simulation output and are not a formal statement; the target is the scoring rule and the exact facts (a)–(e). (c) and (d) were recomputed symbolically when this list was fixed. By (d), adding or subtracting $25/n$ from the printed squared entries is not a valid correction unless the cross term vanishes. The same variance computation is the formal core of finding P029-N009 (the supplement does not say that the RMSEs of the heterogeneous designs and the coverage of Table A6 are measured against each dataset's sample-average effect $S_n$, with $\mathrm{Var}(S_n) = 25/n$, and $250/(9n)$ in the ‘Model is Incorrect’ design); P029-N009 is a reporting omission with no mathematical statement to correct and is not a target in its own right.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: R package icsw 1.0.0 (the published implementation of the method): the compliance-score objective with observation weights and the reweighting bootstrap, set against Section 3.3's ‘bootstrapping the entire process’ and the package help; the witnesses are the validators'
canonical_claim.location: Not in the article PDF. Staged package source: packages/icsw/icsw/R/compliance.score.R, lines 43–48 and 81–92; R/icsw.tsls.R, lines 28–37; man/icsw.tsls.Rd, lines 9–13 and 42–43. The recommendation it implements: p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.3
canonical_claim.statement:
[Statement refuted] (Package help, man/icsw.tsls.Rd, transcribed from the staged file) “Estimate average treatment effects using two-stage least squares with a binary instrument and binary treatment and weighting with inverse complier scores (probabilities of compliance). Optionally, bootstrap the entire estimation process for the purpose of hypothesis testing and constructing confidence intervals.”; argument `weights`: “Observation weights.” Read with the source below, this says that the compliance model is fitted with the supplied observation weights and, in each bootstrap replicate, refitted to that replicate's weights.
[Package source, transcribed from the staged files] One-sided branch (compliance.score.R, lines 43–48): `fit <- glm(D ~ W, df, subset = (Z == 1), family = binomial(link="probit"))`; `C.score <- predict(fit, newdata = df, type = "response")`. Two-sided objective (lines 88–91): `p.D <- p.AC * (1 - p.A) * Z + p.AC * p.A`; `p.D <- pmax(pmin(p.D, 1 - 1e-5), 1e-5)`; `return(-sum(log((p.D)^D * (1 - p.D)^(1 - D) * weights)))`. Bootstrap (icsw.tsls.R, lines 29–32): `weights.r <- rexp(n.obs, 1) # Bayesian bootstrap`; `coefs.r <- icsw.tsls.fit(D, X, Y, Z, W, weights = weights * weights.r, ...`.
[Reading in real arithmetic] With $L_i(\theta) = p_i(\theta)^{D_i}(1 - p_i(\theta))^{1-D_i}$ and $p_i(\theta) \in [10^{-5}, 1 - 10^{-5}]$ the modeled receipt probability of (7), the two-sided objective that is minimized is $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = -\sum_i \log(L_i(\theta)\,w_i)$. The one-sided fit maximizes the unweighted probit likelihood of $D$ on the units with $Z_i = 1$, whatever $w$ is.
[Claims]
(i) For positive finite weights, $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; \mathbf{1}) - \sum_i \log w_i$ for every $\theta$; hence the set of minimizers of $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\cdot; w)$ is the same for every positive $w$, and equals that of the unweighted negative log likelihood.
(ii) If $w_i = 0$ for some $i$ and the other weights are positive, then $L_i(\theta)w_i = 0$ and, with $\log 0 = -\infty$, $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = +\infty$ for every $\theta$.
(iii) [One-sided witness; the final estimate changes] Sixteen observations $(W, Z, D, \text{weight})$: for $W = 0$: four with $(Z, D) = (0, 0)$ and weight $1$; one with $(1, 1)$ and weight $9$; three with $(1, 0)$ and weight $1$; for $W = 1$: four with $(0, 0)$ and weight $1$; three with $(1, 1)$ and weight $9$; one with $(1, 0)$ and weight $1$. $Y = D(1 + W)$. The compliance model has an intercept and the binary predictor $W$ (saturated). The unweighted fit on the $Z = 1$ units gives scores $(C(0), C(1)) = (1/4, 3/4)$, whether or not the weights are supplied. The weighted maximum likelihood fit gives $(9/12, 27/28) = (3/4, 27/28)$. With final weights $u_i = w_i/C(W_i)$ and an intercept as the only covariate, the weighted IV (Wald) estimate is $\frac{\sum_{Z_i=1}u_iY_i}{\sum_{Z_i=1}u_iD_i}$ (the control means of $Y$ and $D$ are $0$): with the package's scores $\frac{36 + 72}{36 + 36} = \frac{3}{2}$; with the weighted scores $\frac{12 + 56}{12 + 28} = \frac{17}{10}$.
(iv) [Two-sided witness] Cells of four observations each, with weight $9$ on every $D = 1$ and weight $1$ on every $D = 0$: $(W, Z) = (0, 0)$: one $D = 1$, three $D = 0$; $(0, 1)$: two and two; $(1, 0)$: one and three; $(1, 1)$: three and one. Writing $q_{xz}$ for the modeled $\Pr(D = 1|W = x, Z = z)$, the nested model with an intercept and $W$ in both equations can realize every $(q_{x0}, q_{x1})$ with $0 < q_{x0} < q_{x1} < 1$. The minimizer of $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}$ (for these or any positive weights) is $q = (q_{00}, q_{01}, q_{10}, q_{11}) = (1/4, 1/2, 1/4, 3/4)$, with compliance scores $q_{x1} - q_{x0} = (1/4, 1/2)$; the maximizer of the weighted likelihood $\prod_i L_i^{w_i}$ is $(3/4, 9/10, 3/4, 27/28)$, with scores $(3/20, 3/14)$. The unweighted likelihood at the second point divided by its value at the first is $729/1500625 < 1$.
(v) [First-step variation omitted by the bootstrap] In the data of (iii) with all weights $1$, change the weight of one $(W, Z, D) = (0, 1, 0)$ observation to $t > 0$. With the scores held at $(1/4, 3/4)$ the weighted IV estimate is $3/2$ for every $t$; with the compliance model refitted to the weights, $C(0) = 1/(3 + t)$, $C(1) = 3/4$ and the estimate is $\frac{t + 11}{t + 7}$, whose derivative at $t = 1$ is $-1/16$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The nested model and likelihood (7): (S6); in the code `p.AC` is $P_{A,C,i}$, `p.A` is $P_{A|A,C,i}$ and `p.D` is the receipt probability of (7), clipped to $[10^{-5}, 1 - 10^{-5}]$. The ICSW estimator and its weighted-2SLS form: (S7); in the package the second stage uses weights `weights / clip.small.probs(scores, min.prob)` (R/icsw.tsls.fit.R), i.e. $u_i = w_i/\hat{P}_{Ci}$ when no score is truncated. Article, p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.3: “To characterize uncertainty, we recommend bootstrapping the entire process—from computing the compliance score to weighted IV estimation (Abadie 2002).” For a cell with weighted numbers $S > 0$ of successes and $F > 0$ of failures, the maximizer of $S\log q + F\log(1 - q)$ on $(0, 1)$ is $S/(S + F)$ (used in (iii)–(v); proved in P029-T8(b)). Not in the article: everything in this target except the quoted recommendation.
canonical_claim.note: P029-E016 is rated an error, Moderate, so this target and P029-T8 have priority 2. It is a finding about the staged package (version 1.0.0, dated 2018-05-16), not about a statement in the article: the article's recommendation is correct and its own replication scripts weight correctly and resample units. It is a target because it rests on exact formal counterexamples, was confirmed in part by two validators (both upheld on re-run), and its correction is a formula (the weighted log likelihood). Witnesses (iii)–(v) are the first validator's (v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2–5; exact_check.py); all numbers were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed. The second validator's witness uses the same sixteen observations with $Y = WD$ and obtains $1/2$ against $7/10$ (v2/artifact/derivation.md), also recomputed. Not established, and not part of the target: that the package's standard errors are too small, any coverage figure, the behaviour of the default (stochastic) two-sided optimizer, whose starting values do depend on the weights, or any error in the article's reported numbers. This statement is transcribed from the staged package files, since it has no page image. The same inside-the-logarithm defect is in the one-sided branch of the Dataverse helper icsw.R (line 50), finding P029-E014 (Minor); claims (i)–(ii) are its formal content as well, and P029-T8 is its corrected statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: R package icsw 1.0.0, compliance-score fit with observation weights, corrected: the weighted log likelihood $-\sum_i w_i\log L_i(\theta)$ (also the corrected one-sided objective of the Dataverse helper, finding P029-E014)
canonical_claim.location: Not in the article PDF. Staged package source: packages/icsw/icsw/R/compliance.score.R, lines 43–47 and 91; Dataverse helper code/dataverse-UCFNHX-v2.0-original/icsw.R, lines 49–50
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected code (validated.json, P029-E016, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] `fit <- glm(D ~ W, df, subset = (Z == 1), weights = weights, family = binomial(link="probit")); return(-sum(weights * log(p.D^D * (1 - p.D)^(1 - D))))`
[Corrected text for the Dataverse helper (validated.json, P029-E014, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “In the deposited icsw.R helper's one-sided branch, minimize -sum_i w_i log L_i(theta), with observation weights outside the logarithm. Omit zero-weight observations before evaluating logs and use the observed-outcome Bernoulli log contribution to handle p.D=0 controls. The canvassing application's direct weighted-probit fits are unaffected.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Let $L_i(\theta) \in (0, 1]$ be the Bernoulli likelihood contribution of observation $i$ ($L_i = p_i^{D_i}(1 - p_i)^{1-D_i}$ with $p_i(\theta) \in (0, 1)$), and $w_i \ge 0$ finite weights. The corrected objective is $Q_{\mathrm{w}}(\theta; w) = -\sum_i w_i\log L_i(\theta)$.
(a) $Q_{\mathrm{w}}(\theta; w)$ is finite for every $\theta$; an observation with $w_i = 0$ contributes $0$; if every $w_i$ is a nonnegative integer, $\exp(-Q_{\mathrm{w}}(\theta; w)) = \prod_i L_i(\theta)^{w_i}$ is the likelihood of the data set in which observation $i$ is repeated $w_i$ times; and $Q_{\mathrm{w}}(\theta; \mathbf{1})$ is the unweighted negative log likelihood.
(b) [Saturated cells] For $S > 0$ and $F > 0$ the function $q \mapsto S\log q + F\log(1 - q)$ on $(0, 1)$ is strictly concave with unique maximizer $q = S/(S + F)$. Hence in a model that fits a free probability $q_c \in (0, 1)$ to each cell $c$, the minimizer of $Q_{\mathrm{w}}$ is $q_c = S_c/(S_c + F_c)$, where $S_c$ and $F_c$ are the sums of the weights of the observations in the cell with $D = 1$ and with $D = 0$ (when both are positive).
(c) [The witnesses of P029-T7 under the corrected objective] In T7(iii) the one-sided fit on the $Z = 1$ units is $(C(0), C(1)) = (3/4, 27/28)$ and the weighted IV estimate is $17/10$; in T7(iv) the fitted receipt probabilities are $(3/4, 9/10, 3/4, 27/28)$, which satisfy $q_{x0} < q_{x1}$, and the compliance scores are $(3/20, 3/14)$; in T7(v) the estimate is $(t + 11)/(t + 7)$.
(d) [Contrast with the printed objective] $Q_{\mathrm{w}}(\theta; w)$ and $Q_{\mathrm{pkg}}(\theta; w) = -\sum_i\log(L_i(\theta)w_i)$ have the same minimizers for every data set and every model if $w$ is constant and positive; for the non-constant weights of T7(iii)–(iv) their minimizers differ.

The weighted IV estimate with final weights $u_i = w_i/C(W_i)$: P029-T7(iii). Not in the article: the whole statement; the article prints only the unweighted likelihood (7).

(b) is the calculation both validators use for their witnesses ($\ell'(q) = \frac{S - (S + F)q}{q(1 - q)}$, $\ell''(q) < 0$). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.1, ‘We see that compliers are more likely to have voted previously, be members of a major party, and identify as white’, read off the correlations of supplement Table A7; the non-identification witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 501 (PDF p. 10), last paragraph; supplement Table A7, p. A11
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement] p. 501: “We see that compliers are more likely to have voted previously, be members of a major party, and identify as white (see the supplementary appendix for a correlation matrix between the estimated compliance score and covariates).” Supplement Table A7 (“Compliance Score / Covariate Correlation Matrix for Green, Gerber and Nickerson (2003). City dummies omitted from columns.”), row ‘Comp. Score’, columns C. Score; Fam. Size; White; Black; Voted 00; Voted 99; Voted Pri.; Age; Age M.; Dem; Rep; Ind: $1.00$; $0.37$; $0.61$; $0.32$; $0.40$; $0.43$; $0.25$; $0.23$; $-0.55$; $0.38$; $0.31$; $-0.47$.
[Inference refuted] That the recorded data determine the sign of the pooled association between being a complier and identifying as white. In the staged data the indicator ‘White’ is $1$ exactly for records whose race field is ‘W’; the race field is blank for every record outside Raleigh.
[Counts from the staged data (the validator's; recomputed from the staged file when this list was fixed)] $N = 18933$ records, of which $4660$ are in Raleigh ($3884$ with race W, $776$ with another or an unknown code) and $14273$ are in the five other cities, all with a blank race field. $8721$ records are assigned to treatment and $2551$ of them were contacted; no control record was contacted. Among the Raleigh records assigned to treatment, $602$ of the $1370$ recorded W and $160$ of the $315$ others were contacted.
[Sign identity] For a finite population of $N$ units with binary variables $W$ and $C$, let $n_W = \#\{W = 1\}$, $n_C = \#\{C = 1\}$ and $n_{11} = \#\{W = 1, C = 1\}$, with $0 < n_W < N$. Then, with population (denominator $N$) moments, $\mathrm{Cov}(C, W) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{N^2}$ and $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{n_W(N - n_W)}$; both have the sign of $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W$.
[Two complete populations compatible with the same recorded data] In both, each record assigned to treatment has $C_i$ equal to its recorded contact indicator and each control record has $C_i = 0$, with $D_i(0) = 0$ and $D_i(1) = C_i$ (so the recorded $D_i = Z_iC_i$ is reproduced, there are no defiers and noncompliance is one-sided), and $Y_i(0) = Y_i(1)$ equal to the recorded outcome; every recorded race code is kept, and the $21$ Raleigh records with an unknown code are non-white. World A: every record with a blank race field is non-white. World B: every record with a blank race field is white.
(A) $N = 18933$, $n_W = 3884$, $n_C = 2551$, $n_{11} = 602$: $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W = 1489582 > 0$ and $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = \dfrac{744791}{29225158} > 0$.
(B) $N = 18933$, $n_W = 3884 + 14273 = 18157$, $n_C = 2551$, $n_{11} = 602 + (2551 - 762) = 2391$: $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W = -1049704 < 0$ and $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = -\dfrac{131213}{1761229} < 0$.
Hence the recorded data are compatible both with compliers being more likely, and with compliers being less likely, to be white than non-compliers.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Compliers and $D_0$, $D_1$: (S1)–(S2); here $C_i = \mathbf{1}\{D_{1i} > D_{0i}\}$. The application has one-sided noncompliance (p. 500, PDF p. 9: “Because some citizens who were assigned to the treatment group could not be contacted, the study features one-sided noncompliance.”). The indicator in the replication script (transcribed from the staged greengerbernickerson.R): `white <- race == "W"`. The count $762 = 602 + 160$ is the number of contacted records among the $1685$ Raleigh records assigned to treatment. Not in the paper: the counts, the identity and both completions (the validator's derivation.md, sections 3, 5 and 7).
canonical_claim.note: P029-N004 is rated an error, Moderate; it is an interpretive finding, listed because it rests on an exact non-identification argument, as the brief provides. Sol's verdict is confirmed_in_part, upheld on re-run: what is established is that the race and party characterisation is not supported by the cited correlations (blank labels are coded zero and their availability varies by city); it is not established that the true pooled comparison is negative, and both falsity flags in the verdict are false for that reason. The correlations of Table A7 are numerically right and the ‘voted previously’ part of the sentence stands. All counts in this target were recomputed from the staged greengerbernickerson.dta when this list was fixed, and (A) and (B) by integer arithmetic. The validator gives an analogous pair of completions for the party labels (blank in Detroit, Minneapolis and St. Paul and for 489 Columbus records): with the source-coded major-party indicator $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W = 2225222$ ($n_W = 5221$, $n_{11} = 821$), and $-20919602$ when blank party fields are completed as major-party exactly for $C = 0$ ($n_W = 14279$, $n_{11} = 819$, starting from the indicator that excludes the code LIB); these are in exact_output.txt and are not part of the formal statement. The statements about fitted compliance scores (the within-Raleigh correlation $-0.41$, the between- and within-city covariances) depend on a numerical probit fit and are not formal targets.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.1, description of the compliers, corrected (formal content of the narrowed claim): what the recorded race labels do and do not determine
canonical_claim.location: p. 501 (PDF p. 10), last paragraph; supplement Table A7, p. A11
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text (validated.json, P029-N004, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Estimated compliance scores are positively associated with prior voting. The pooled correlations with recorded White and major-party indicators also reflect differences between cities in contact rates and covariate availability. Within Raleigh, the only city supplying race labels, voters recorded as White have lower mean estimated compliance scores than the remaining records. Table A7 note: Blank race and party labels are coded zero in the respective indicators; race is unavailable outside Raleigh and party is unavailable throughout Detroit, Minneapolis, and St. Paul, with additional blank party records in Columbus. Age, primary-vote history, and 1999-vote history are unavailable in particular cities and are imputed.”
[Formal content, with every hypothesis]
(a) [What decides the sign] For a finite population of $N$ units with binary $W$ and $C$ and counts $n_W$, $n_C$, $n_{11}$ as in P029-T9, with $0 < n_W < N$ and $0 < n_C < N$: $\mathrm{Cov}(C, W) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{N^2}$, $\mathrm{E}(C|W = 1) - \mathrm{E}(C|W = 0) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{n_W(N - n_W)}$ and $\mathrm{E}(W|C = 1) - \mathrm{E}(W|C = 0) = \dfrac{Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W}{n_C(N - n_C)}$. So ‘compliers are more likely to be white’ and ‘white units are more likely to be compliers’ are both equivalent to $Nn_{11} > n_Cn_W$.
(b) [What the recorded labels show where they exist] Among the $1685$ Raleigh records assigned to treatment, where contact reveals compliance, the contact rate of records with race W is $602/1370$ and that of the other records is $160/315$; $\dfrac{602}{1370} - \dfrac{160}{315} = -\dfrac{2957}{43155} < 0$. Excluding the $7$ treatment-assigned records with an unknown race code ($5$ of them contacted): $\dfrac{602}{1370} - \dfrac{155}{308} = -\dfrac{13467}{210980} < 0$.
(c) [What the recorded data do not determine] The sign of the pooled association between compliance and race over the six cities is not determined by the recorded data: the two completions of P029-T9 agree on every recorded value and give $Nn_{11} - n_Cn_W = 1489582$ and $-1049704$.
(d) [Why a pooled correlation with a recorded-label indicator can differ in sign from the within-city one] For a finite population partitioned into groups, with $\bar{s}_G$ and $\bar{A}_G$ the means of $s$ and $A$ in the group $G$ of a unit and all moments taken with denominator $N$: $\mathrm{Cov}(s, A) = \mathrm{E}[(s - \bar{s}_G)(A - \bar{A}_G)] + \mathrm{E}[(\bar{s}_G - \bar{s})(\bar{A}_G - \bar{A})]$. If $A$ is constant within every group but one, the first (within-group) term is $n_G/N$ times the covariance of $s$ and $A$ inside that group.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The counts and the two completions: P029-T9. $s$ stands for the estimated compliance score and $A$ for a recorded indicator (White, Dem, Rep, Ind), the groups being the six cities; the indicator White is zero outside Raleigh. Not in the paper: (a)–(d) (the validator's derivation.md, sections 5–7).
